about.title: Compton Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A wet aisle in a grocery store on Alondra Boulevard. A cracked walkway outside an apartment building near Wilmington Avenue. A parking lot off Rosecrans Avenue where the lighting quit working weeks ago. Falls like these happen quietly across Compton, and the people they hurt are often left wondering whether anyone is actually responsible. Under California law, a property owner is not automatically at fault just because you fell. What matters is notice: whether the owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and then failed to fix it or warn you. That question sits at the heart of most premises liability claims in Los Angeles County. LawProactive is not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Compton residents with an independent personal injury attorney who handles slip-and-fall and premises cases. There is no charge to be matched, and the attorneys in our network work on contingency, so you owe nothing unless your case results in a recovery. If you were hurt on someone else's property, documenting the hazard early makes a real difference.

whyChoose.title: Why Compton Residents Use LawProactive for Premises Claims

items.title: Attorneys who understand the notice requirement
items.desc: California premises cases turn on whether the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to fix or warn. The attorneys we connect you with know how to look for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that speak to that question.

items.title: Help preserving video before it disappears
items.desc: Many Compton stores and apartment complexes keep surveillance footage for only days or weeks. An attorney can send a preservation demand quickly so the recording of your fall is not overwritten.

items.title: Clear guidance on deadlines and shared fault
items.desc: You generally have two years to file against a private owner, and far less time if a public entity is involved. California's pure comparative fault rule also means a claim is not lost just because an insurer says you were partly to blame.

items.question: I fell on a broken sidewalk in Compton. Does the two-year deadline still apply?
items.answer: Not necessarily. If the sidewalk or property is owned or maintained by the City of Compton, Los Angeles County, or another public entity, California requires a government claim to be filed first, typically within six months of the injury. That is a much tighter window than the two years allowed for claims against private owners. Because ownership of a sidewalk or public lot is not always obvious, it helps to speak with an attorney early.

items.question: The store manager says I should have watched where I was walking. Can I still bring a claim?
items.answer: Possibly. California follows pure comparative fault, which means your recovery can be reduced by your share of responsibility but is not eliminated by it. If a hazard existed and the owner knew or should have known about it, the fact that you were carrying bags or looking at a shelf does not end the conversation. An attorney can evaluate how the facts line up.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall on someone else's property?
items.answer: Get medical care first, even if the pain seems minor at the time. If you are able, photograph the hazard, the surrounding area, and anything like missing warning signs or poor lighting, and ask for an incident report. Write down the names of any witnesses. Then reach out so an attorney can request surveillance video before it is deleted.
